research_question: How can the linear threshold model of influence diffusion be extended to two competing technologies so that a player can choose early adopters to maximize its own spread, and does the greedy (1-1/e) approximation for influence maximization still apply to these competitive extensions?
theory: Extends the Kempe-Kleinberg-Tardos linear threshold model with competition. Four variants are proposed: a weight-proportional model where active neighbours of either technology share one threshold and adoption is split by weight; a separated-threshold model with technology-specific weights and thresholds; a forcing extension in which remaining inactive nodes adopt a technology at a final step; and an OR model where each technology spreads independently and a decision function chooses between them at the end, with a repeated-OR variant. Key properties studied are monotonicity and submodularity of the expected A-spread, which determine whether the Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher greedy guarantee applies.
data: No empirical data. Theoretical instances: directed graph G=(V,E) with per-technology edge weights in [0,1] whose incoming weights sum to at most 1, initial adopter sets for A and B, a budget k, and node thresholds drawn uniformly from [0,1] (or intervals). Sample sizes are illustrative trees and graphs in Figures 1-2 (for example a 7-node tree for the monotonicity counterexample). The hardness reduction builds a graph with N = O(n^(2 alpha+2)) nodes from a Vertex Cover instance.
method: Formal model definitions; monotonicity and submodularity counterexamples on small trees (Theorems 1-2, 4, 6; Appendices A, C); an inductive coupling proof over fixed thresholds and coin flips for monotonicity of the separated-threshold model (Lemma 3, Theorem 3, Appendix B); a live-edge equivalence argument for submodularity of the OR model (Lemma 2); a reduction from Vertex Cover for NP-hardness of approximation (Theorems 7-8, Appendix D); and application of Mossel-Roch's result for generalized submodular thresholds (Theorems 10-11).
scope: Abstract directed weighted social networks of arbitrary size; no population, institution or era. Main text uses two competing technologies, with a claim (no proof given) that results extend to several. Time is discrete steps with no calendar period. Results are worst-case or existence statements, not average-case.
measures: Expected number of A-active nodes sigma(IA, IB) at termination
Per-node activation probabilities alpha and beta at step t, and their values after adding a seed x

key_findings.finding: Weight-proportional competitive linear threshold model is not monotone: adding an A seed can lower the spread of A.
key_findings.location: Section 2, Theorem 1; proof in Appendix A, Theorem 12 with Figure 1(a)
key_findings.numbers: Node r activation probability for A: 11/40 before and 103/400 after adding a seed (0.275 vs 0.2575)

key_findings.finding: Weight-proportional model is also not submodular.
key_findings.location: Section 2, Theorem 2; proof in Appendix A, Theorem 13 with Figure 1(b)
key_findings.numbers: For S={w} vs T={w,y} (probabilities 3/10 to 17/60 for S; 7/10 to 17/50 for T)

key_findings.finding: Separated-threshold model is monotone: adding A seeds never reduces the probability a node becomes A-active at any step, and never raises the probability of B.
key_findings.location: Section 3, Theorem 3; proof in Appendix B, Lemma 3 and Theorem 14
key_findings.numbers: None; qualitative inequality alpha-hat at step t >= alpha at step t

key_findings.finding: Separated-threshold model is not submodular in general; the claimed counterexample is only in a full version not included in this text.
Adding a forcing step keeps monotonicity-type properties but does not restore submodularity; the result holds for any tie-breaking and any forcing rule.
key_findings.location: Section 4, Theorem 5 (monotonicity) and Theorem 6 (non-submodularity); counterexample in Appendix C, Figure 2
key_findings.numbers: Forced-model counterexample: A-probability at root 0 for S and 0 for T, but 1 for T with the added seed, violating submodularity

key_findings.finding: Separated-threshold competitive problem is NP-hard to approximate within a factor better than N^(1/2 - eps), for any eps > 0.
key_findings.location: Section 5, Theorem 7; reduction in Appendix D, Theorem 16 from Vertex Cover
key_findings.numbers: Ratio bound Omega(N^(1/2 - eps)); gap exponent (alpha+3)/(2 alpha+2) tends to 1/2 with beta = alpha+2

key_findings.finding: Same hardness applies to the separate-edge-weight Wave Propagation model of Carnes et al., giving a negative answer to their conjecture that the process remains monotone and submodular.
key_findings.location: Section 5, Theorem 8 and the paragraph before it; reference to Carnes et al. 2007

key_findings.finding: OR model (technologies spread independently, then a decision step with monotone submodular decision functions) is monotone and submodular in the A-spread.
Greedy (1-1/e-eps) approximation is achievable for the OR model and its generalized version with any monotone submodular node-level functions.

Repeating the OR process for several iterations (e.g. daily spread in an election, with edge weights possibly changing between iterations) with one final decision step remains monotone and submodular.
key_findings.numbers: Number of iterations l is arbitrary; no numeric bound

key_findings.finding: Authors argue that no single true model exists and suggest game-theoretic settings where competing firms bid for strategic nodes.

limitations: Theorem 4 (separated-threshold non-submodularity) is stated without proof; the counterexample is said to appear only in a full version on the authors' websites.
Proof of Lemma 3 is omitted for lack of space and deferred to the full version.
Main text treats two technologies; extension to several is asserted, not proven.
Hardness results are asymptotic worst-case bounds (N^(1/2 - eps)); they do not characterize typical instances or give an algorithm.

Greedy guarantee applies only to the OR model (and generalized OR) under monotone submodular decision functions; the paper concedes most other models are unfit for the Nemhauser et al. technique and leaves open whether efficient approximations exist.
Model is one-shot diffusion with uniformly random thresholds; partial-knowledge intervals are mentioned but not analyzed.
No empirical validation of any model on real networks or election data.
